[0] Privacy search engine DuckDuckGo has released a new survey revealing how much personal information users are sharing with AI chatbots, and how many people are unaware of what happens to these conversations. Here are the details.

[1] Survey Shows AI Users Share More Than They Realize

[2] A survey published today by DuckDuckGo reveals several privacy concerns about how people use AI chatbots, including the finding that nearly one-third of users have told an AI something they wouldn't share with a friend, family member, colleague, or medical professional. Among those who identify as AI enthusiasts, this figure rises to 56%.

[3] Here's what DuckDuckGo had to say:

[4] The company noted that out of nearly 2,000 U.S. adult respondents, 53% didn't know or weren't sure that most chatbots use conversations by default to train models, and only 25% knew that AI conversations can be subpoenaed by law enforcement.

[5] The results also revealed significant behavioral differences between parents and non-parents, with parents or guardians in households with children nearly twice as likely to confide in AI compared to non-parents. DuckDuckGo stated that "among parents using AI, 43% have told an AI something they've never shared with anyone," while "for AI users without children in the home, that figure drops to 25%."

[6] DuckDuckGo believes that AI companies, through advertising and media exposure, encourage users to treat chatbots as confidants, even though these conversations may not be as private as users are led to believe.

[7] When it comes to trust, the survey found that people have slightly more confidence in large AI companies to protect their data than they do in the U.S. government. However, skepticism toward both is high: 39% expressed no trust at all in large AI companies, while 48% had no trust at all in the government.

[8] DuckDuckGo concluded by noting that users still have an opportunity to change how they approach AI privacy, especially since chatbot usage is still relatively new:

[9] When it comes to online privacy with search engines and browsers, many people think, "It's too late; my data has already been exposed." But the most valuable information you can share with Big Tech is actually your next question, not the questions you asked days, months, or years ago. So it's never too late to switch to more privacy-focused online services.

[10] The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data handling policies.
